kurz: How a stock market crash turned into a banking crisis, why the central bank reacted wrongly and which institutions from these four years still exist today.

bloecke.md:
The boom of the 1920s had real foundations. Electrification, the assembly line, radio and the automobile raised the productivity of American industry, profits rose, and investors who had bought shares in 1921 owned a multiple of their stake eight years later. Great excesses almost always begin with an accurate observation. What proved fatal in this case was the type of financing.

Shares were bought on credit to an extent that is hard to imagine today. In 1929, more than $8.5 billion in [[Securities-backed loan|securities-backed loans]] was outstanding in the USA, more than the entire stock of cash then in circulation. Brokers routinely financed more than two thirds of the purchase price, and a down payment of one third was considered solid. On 3 September 1929, the Dow Jones reached its peak with a closing level of 381.17 points.

bloecke.formel: Loss on equity = price loss ÷ equity ratio
bloecke.erklaerung: A loan leaves the risk of the security unchanged and changes the yardstick against which it is measured. Leverage works exactly symmetrically. The loss side, however, ends at zero equity, while the gain side has no limit.

bloecke.beispiel: With a down payment of 30%, a 30% fall in the price wipes out all the equity: 0.30 ÷ 0.30 = 1. If the price falls by 35%, a residual debt also remains after the forced sale.

bloecke.md: This describes the basic outline of what happened in October 1929. If the value of the collateral falls below the agreed limit, the broker makes a margin call. If the investor does not pay, their securities are sold, regardless of how valuable anyone considers the company to be. The selling pressure therefore arises from the loan agreements. That is why the prices of sound companies also fall in such phases, because whatever can be sold is sold.

bloecke.titel: Course of the crisis and the recovery
bloecke.unter: The stock market crash lasted a few days, the crisis four years and the return of the index to its old level a quarter of a century.

ereignisse.text: 3 September: The Dow Jones reaches its peak. Securities-backed loans stand at over $8.5 billion.
24 October: 12.9 million shares are traded. On 28 October the index falls by 12.82%, and on 29 October by 11.73% with 16.4 million shares traded.

ereignisse.titel: Smoot-Hawley and the first wave of bank failures
ereignisse.text: The US tariff triggers a series of retaliatory tariffs worldwide. Consumer prices fall by 2.3%.
In May, Austria's Creditanstalt collapses. In July, the Danatbank (Darmstädter und Nationalbank) closes, and bank holidays are imposed in Germany.
8 July: The Dow Jones stands 89.2% below its 1929 peak. In February, over 6 million people in Germany are unemployed.
In March, all banks nationwide are closed. Deposit protection, the separation of commercial and investment banking and the departure from the gold standard follow.
Monetary and fiscal policy are tightened too early. The stock market loses 54.5% in 12.8 months.
23 November: For the first time, the Dow closes above its 1929 level again, in nominal terms and without dividends.

bloecke.md:
The well-known crash days together cost around 23%. However, most of the loss occurred in the just over 32 months that followed. Prices fell in small steps, interrupted by recoveries that were interpreted as the turning point each time. On 8 July 1932, the Dow stood at 41.22 points. Investors who had bought in October 1929 because prices now seemed low went on to lose most of their stake once more.

The fact that contemporaries did not recognise this development was not due to a lack of intelligence. Even the most eminent American economist of his time had publicly declared the opposite a few days before the crash.

bloecke.text: Stock prices have reached what looks like a permanently high plateau.

bloecke.md:
## From stock market crisis to banking crisis

What happened in the credit system weighed more heavily. Between 1930 and 1933, around a third of all American banks disappeared. There was no [[Deposit protection|deposit protection]], and savers whose bank collapsed lost their money. That is why many withdrew their money from all banks as a precaution. But banks do not keep deposits in the vault; they lend them on. In this way, a decision that was sensible for each individual brought the whole system to a standstill. The money supply shrank by about 30%.

The central bank did not intervene. In October 1931, the Fed even raised interest rates in order to keep the dollar tied to gold after Britain had left the gold standard. This happened in the middle of the most severe contraction in economic history. Nobody took on the role of the [[Lender of last resort|lender of last resort]], which Walter Bagehot had already described in 1873.

bloecke.titel: US consumer prices 1926-1940, change on the previous year
bloecke.unter: After four years of falling prices, the price level in 1933 was around a quarter below that of 1929.

bloecke.md: For savers, falling prices sound pleasant at first. For debtors, however, they are a heavy burden, and in a credit economy almost everyone is a debtor. In 1933, Irving Fisher described this relationship as debt deflation. The debt is fixed in nominal terms, while the income from which it is serviced shrinks with the price level. Debtors who want to repay have to sell, and in doing so they push prices down further.

The annual rates for 1930 to 1933 (−2.3%, −9.0%, −9.9%, −5.1%) give a cumulative fall in the price level of around 24%: 0.977 × 0.910 × 0.901 × 0.949 ≈ 0.760.

A loan of $100,000 taken out in 1929 therefore corresponded to a real burden of around $132,000 in 1933, even though not a single additional dollar had been borrowed. With a nominal interest rate of 5% and a 10% fall in prices, the real interest rate is around 16.7% (1.05 ÷ 0.90 ≈ 1.167). This explains why it was deflation that created the Depression, and not the stock market crash.

bloecke.unter: Each individual step is rational for the person taking it, but together the steps form a cycle that nobody can stop alone.

bloecke.md:
## Spread to Europe and Germany

The Smoot-Hawley Tariff of 1930 turned the American crisis into a global one. Trading partners responded with tariffs of their own, and world trade shrank. Europe was also dependent on short-term US loans, which were now being called in. In May 1931, Austria's Creditanstalt collapsed, and in July 1931 the Danatbank (Darmstädter und Nationalbank). Bank holidays and foreign exchange controls followed.

The slumps in the USA and Germany were similarly severe. Industrial production fell by 46.8% in the USA and by 41.8% in Germany. In Germany, the number of unemployed rose from around 1.9 million on average in 1929 to over 6 million in February 1932, and the unemployment rate in the USA rose to around 25%. Chancellor Brüning used emergency decrees to reinforce what was happening anyway. He cut wages, salaries and government spending in order to maintain the gold parity of the Reichsmark. The memory of 1923, which is the subject of the next lesson, made any monetary easing politically impossible. Germany therefore fought deflation with the tools of fighting inflation.

## Lasting reforms of the New Deal

The most important break came in March 1933. Roosevelt had all banks closed for a few days and inspected; only the solvent ones were allowed to reopen. This ended the withdrawal of deposits. State deposit protection, the separation of lending and securities business and the break with the gold standard followed in the same year. In January 1934, on the basis of the Gold Reserve Act, the gold price was raised from $20.67 to $35 per fine ounce, which in effect amounted to a devaluation of the dollar. In 1934, the SEC was added as the securities regulator, together with rules on minimum margins for securities-backed loans.

Whether the New Deal's job creation programmes carried the recovery is still disputed today. It is largely undisputed, by contrast, that countries that left the gold standard early emerged from the Depression earlier. According to this view, the turning point came with the end of the gold peg that the countries had imposed on themselves.

In 1936/37, the situation seemed stable enough to raise minimum reserves and consolidate the budget. The stock market then lost 54.5% in 12.8 months, and unemployment rose again. The old peak of 1937 was not reached again until 1946. This experience explains why central banks kept monetary policy loose for so long after 2008 and 2020. In central banks' textbooks, the fear of a second 1937 weighs more heavily than the fear of 2% too much inflation.

bloecke.titel: Depth and duration of major market declines compared with 1929 (S&P 500 or its predecessor index)

bloecke.md:
The table puts two reassuring assumptions into perspective. First, the depth of a decline says little about how long the recovery will take. The coronavirus slump was deeper than the decline in the 2022 interest rate shock, but it was made up four times as fast. Second, the statement “the market always comes back” is true, but it is of little help as long as it remains unclear how long an investor has to hold out.

The 25 years to 1954 are nevertheless among the most frequently misused figures in financial history. They apply to a price return index without dividends, calculated in nominal dollars. Dividend yields were high at the time, and, by calculation, the purchasing power of a dollar rose by around a third between 1929 and 1933. A broadly diversified investor who kept collecting and reinvesting the dividends was therefore back in profit considerably earlier than the chart suggests. This does not play down the crisis, but it shows that you have to read a chart carefully before drawing conclusions from it.

After a loss of 89.2%, 10.8% of the stake is left. To get back to 100, this remainder has to grow more than ninefold: 1 ÷ 0.108 ≈ 9.26, that is, a gain of around 826%. Losses and the gains needed to make up for them are not symmetrical. This is the main reason to avoid leverage.

## Lessons for monetary policy

Four consequences still shape monetary policy today. First, in a panic the central bank provides liquidity, if necessary without limit. In 2020, the Fed cut its key interest rate to 0-0.25% within days and announced bond purchases of $700 billion. Second, deposits are guaranteed so that a bank run does not even begin. Third, no rigid exchange rate target may force monetary policy to tighten in a recession. Fourth, the inflation target is 2% rather than zero. In its strategy of July 2021, the ECB expressly justifies this with the safety margin against deflation and the lower bound on interest rates, a direct lesson from 1931.

Whether the central bank bears the main blame has not been conclusively settled by research. But the direction of the verdict is clear. No school of economic thought today still considers it justifiable to let the money supply shrink by 30% while a third of the banks disappear.

According to the **monetarist** explanation (Friedman/Schwartz, *A Monetary History*, 1963), the Depression was a failure of the Fed. Without the contraction of the money supply, the recession of 1929 would have remained an ordinary recession.

The **Keynesian** explanation sees the cause in the collapse of private demand and investment. According to this view, monetary policy alone could have achieved little at the lower bound on interest rates.

According to the **institutional** explanation (Eichengreen, Temin), the gold standard transmitted the crisis from country to country and prevented individual countries from countering it with their own monetary policy. The order in which countries left the gold standard is a good predictor of the order of their recovery.

The **credit channel** explanation (Bernanke, 1983) emphasises that when the banks disappeared, the knowledge of who was creditworthy disappeared with them. This information could not be replaced quickly. That is why lending remained weak even when money was available again.

The four explanations contradict each other less than the debate suggests. They weight the same causes differently.

- Balances and securities are treated differently in law. Account balances are covered by statutory deposit protection of €100,000 per customer and institution under Section 8 EinSiG (Deposit Guarantee Act). Securities in a securities account, by contrast, belong to the customer and do not become part of the insolvency estate if the bank becomes insolvent (DepotG, Securities Deposit Act). Deposit protection is neither necessary nor applicable to them.
- An obligation to make additional payments (Nachschusspflicht) hardly exists any more for private investors. BaFin (Federal Financial Supervisory Authority) has prohibited it for CFDs, and leverage is capped depending on the underlying. However, a conventional securities-backed loan against the portfolio still provides for the realisation of the collateral. The mechanism of 1929 therefore still exists, albeit within narrower limits.
- Losses only have a tax effect to the extent that matching gains arise. Under Section 20(6) sentence 4 EStG (Income Tax Act), losses from share sales may only be offset against gains from share sales. The bank offsets them immediately against such gains in the same calendar year, including gains realised earlier in the year (Section 43a(3) sentence 2 EStG). Unused losses are carried forward indefinitely; carrying them back is not possible. The saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) is €1,000 (Section 20(9) EStG). A tax refund therefore softens a crash immediately to the extent that matching gains have already arisen in the same year, and otherwise only with later gains.

mitnehmen: A loan can turn a fall in prices into a predicament, because with a down payment of one third, a price loss of one third wipes out all the equity.
The crash days in October 1929 cost around 23%, and afterwards the Dow fell by around another 82% in the just under three years to the 1932 low.
The Depression was caused by the bank failures, the money supply shrinking by 30% and four years of falling prices, not by the stock market crash.
Deposit protection, the lender of last resort and an inflation target of 2% rather than zero are institutional responses to the years 1929 to 1933.

The 25 years to 1954 apply to a price return index without dividends in nominal dollars, whereas a diversified portfolio with distributions, taking deflation into account, was back in profit considerably earlier.

begriffe.text: Loan secured by the portfolio that finances the purchase of further securities. If the portfolio value falls below the agreed limit, the lender makes a margin call or realises the position, regardless of how the investor assesses the situation.
Cycle described by Irving Fisher in 1933 in which falling prices increase the real burden of debts fixed in nominal terms. Debtors sell in order to repay and thereby push prices down further.
Role of the central bank in providing unlimited liquidity to solvent banks against good collateral during a panic. It was not performed in the years 1930 to 1933; since then it has been standard.
Statutory guarantee for bank balances, in Germany up to €100,000 per customer and institution under Section 8 EinSiG. In the USA, it was introduced in 1933 in response to the bank runs.
